activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story: Theodore went to the store with Mama. He wanted a cookie from the bakery. He held Mama's hand in the middle of the aisle. But the bakery was dark. The big oven was cold. No cookies today, said the baker. We bake them tomorrow. Theodore looked at the dark oven. He kicked his shoe on the floor, just a little kick. Yesterday we had cookies, said Mama. Today the oven is cold. Tomorrow we will come back. Theodore looked at the bread shelf. He picked a soft roll instead. He held it in both hands. Now he had something to eat. Later, at home, Mama put jam on it. Theodore took a big bite. Tomorrow we get cookies, he said. And tomorrow he did.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Leon sat on the big red couch at Mr. Kay's house. Everyone was watching the big game on TV. Leon took a bite of his cheese snack. It was good.

Then the team got close to scoring. Everyone jumped up. "GO! GO! GO!" they all yelled. Grandpa yelled too. Aunt Millie yelled loudest of all. Leon covered his ears. Then the room got quiet. The TV man said, "We missed the play while you cheered!" Leon looked at the frozen picture on the screen. He thought and thought.

"Wait," said Leon. "When we yell, we can't hear the game." Mr. Kay laughed. "That's right, little buddy!" So Leon held up his hand like a traffic helper. "Yell now!" he said when there was a break. Everyone yelled like wild bears. "Shhh now," said Leon when the game came back. Aunt Millie tied a string on her wrist to remind her.

The team scored the last point. Leon jumped high. "NOW we can yell!" he shouted. And everyone did.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Daniel was at the little stove in his school cooking classroom. He was making muffins for his family. Mama would get the big one. Baby sister would get the tiny one.

Daniel mixed flour and milk in a big bowl. He cracked an egg. Some shell fell in. "Got you," he said, and fished it out with a spoon. Then he filled his muffin cups and set them in the oven to bake.

The timer rang. Daniel pulled the pan out with safe, big mitts on. But the muffins were flat like pancakes. Flat, flat, flat. He looked at the counter. A small jar sat there all alone. "The puffy stuff!" he said. He had left the baking soda in the jar. No puffy stuff, no puffy muffins. He laughed and laughed. Then he mixed a new bowl, tapped the baking soda in, and those muffins came out big as clouds. He put them in a basket and ran to find his teacher. "Look! Puff magic!"

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Luca ran out to the backyard. He wanted to find his red ball. It was not in the toy box. He looked behind the big green bush. No ball there.

Then he heard a happy sound. "Tweet, tweet!" A blue bird flew by. Luca followed it. The bird landed by the flower bed. And there was the red ball, sitting under a yellow flower!

Luca picked up his ball. It was dirty. "I will clean it," he said. He wiped it with a wet cloth. The ball turned bright and shiny again. Luca held it up high. "The bird took my ball to the flowers!" he said. "That is why I could not find it!" He laughed and kicked the ball across the green, green grass.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Wesley stood in the band room. A shiny trumpet sat on the stand. He wanted to play it for his mom today.

He took a big, big breath. He blew as hard as he could. Pfffffft. Nothing. Not one sound. Just air. He tried again. Harder! Pfffffft. Still nothing. A cymbal fell over with a clang.

Miss Paz came over. "Try little air," she said. "Tiny, tiny air."

Wesley took a small breath. He blew softly. Bzzzz! A sound came out! A big, funny sound. "Loud air makes no sound," said Wesley. "Little air makes the sound!"

Miss Paz laughed. He played again. Bzzzz! Bzzzz! His arms wanted to swing like a drummer's.

Then it was time to go. His mom was waiting. "Play for me!" she said. Wesley lifted the trumpet. He blew tiny air. Bzzzz!

His mom clapped and clapped. "Bravo!" she said. "After this, we can eat crunchy crackers at home."

Wesley grinned. Little air, big sound. He liked that trick.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story: John sat at the big art table. He wanted to make a house picture. He cut out a square for the house. He cut out a rectangle for the door. He cut out a triangle for the roof. Then he cut a circle for the sun. John put the circle on the table. The circle rolled off! It rolled under the chair. "My sun ran away," said John. His teacher helped him look. "Round things roll," John said. He picked up the circle with his finger. The teacher was melting crayons for a bright sun picture. "Careful," she said. "The warm wax can burn." John watched and waited. She poured red and yellow wax. It made a curly, swirly sun. John taped his square, rectangle and triangle flat on the paper. They did not roll at all. Then he pressed the curly sun on top. "Flat sides stay put," said John. "Only round things roll."

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Myles ran into the backyard. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. He wore his sun hat and his cool sunglasses. A turtle sat by the fence, in the warm sun.

Then the wind came. Whoosh! The wind blew Myles's hat right off his head. The hat flew over the grass. "Come back!" said Myles. He chased it and caught it. "Why did you fly?" he asked the hat.

Myles looked up. The wind pushed the tree leaves too. The leaves waved and waved. "The wind moves things," said Myles. "That is why my hat flew!" So he put the hat on and tied the strap under his chin. Snug!

Rain began to fall. Myles ran inside. He grabbed his rain boots and his yellow rain coat. He looked out the window. "Maybe tomorrow it will be snowy," he said. "Then I need my big warm mittens, so my hands will not freeze." The rain went drip, drip, drip on the glass. Myles watched and smiled.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Camille wanted to help Mama make soup. "Stay close to me," said Mama. Camille stood right by her side. One step, two steps, close to Mama.

The pot went on the stove. Steam rose up, up, up. Camille put her hand near the steam. The air felt hot. She pulled her hand back fast. "The steam is hot," said Camille. "My hand went away because it was hot." Mama nodded and smiled. Camille touched the cold jug of water instead. Cold felt nice and safe.

Then Camille saw the big knife on the counter. She did not touch it. "That is not for me," she said. She was a brave helper, and Mama let her fill the cups with cold water. One cup, two cups, three cups. "My dream is to cook like you," said Camille. Mama laughed softly and gave her a big warm hug.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Madison wanted to paint a green snake. She had red, blue and yellow paint. But there was no green paint at all. She looked and looked. No green anywhere.

She painted one snake red. She painted one snake blue. Then she painted a big yellow snake. She still wanted a green snake. So she dipped her brush in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow too. She stirred the paints on the paper. "Ooh!" said Madison. Blue and yellow made green! The green spread like magic grass.

"Green snake, green snake, come out to play," she sang. She made three green snakes. Then she shut her paint box tight. The snakes slid across the paper, all the way to the flower garden. "Because blue and yellow mix," said Madison, "green snakes can live in my yard."

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
story:
Sophie sat in the car. She held a cookie in her hand. Today was a big day. Mom was bringing the baby home.

The baby had a small seat. The small seat faced the back of the car. Sophie looked and looked. She could not see the baby. "I want to see the baby," she said.

Dad counted the seats. "One, two, three," he said. "Try the middle seat." Sophie climbed over. She sat in the middle. Now she could see the baby's face. The baby was sleeping. "The baby sleeps because the car goes bumpy bumpy," said Sophie. "The bumps rock her, like my doll."

Mom smiled. Sophie took a deep breath. She whispered very softly. "Hi, baby. I am Sophie." The baby opened one eye. Then she made a small sound. Sophie broke her cookie in two. She kept one half. She saved one half for the baby, for later. "When you wake up," she whispered, "we will count things together. One cookie. Two cookies. Just you wait."

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Benjamin wants to play house at daycare. He picks a doll to be his baby. The baby will not sleep. It keeps "crying" in his arms.

"You need a blanket," says Mia. She folds a small red cloth. Benjamin wraps the baby up. The baby gets warm and cozy. Now it stops crying and sleeps.

"It slept because it was warm," Benjamin says.

Next, the baby is hungry. Benjamin makes pretend soup from a cup and a leaf. The baby eats it all up. Then a big block tower falls down with a crash. It sounds like thunder. The baby looks scared. Benjamin hugs it close.

"Shh. That was just a mountain falling," he says. He rocks the baby. The baby falls asleep again. Benjamin smiles and tucks the blanket in tight.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
The big family dinner was ready at Grandma's house. Aurora could smell the warm bread. She wanted to hurry to the table and eat.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "We hold hands first. Then we say our blessing together." Everyone stood around the table. Grandma took Aurora's hand. Papa took her other hand. Every person held on to someone.

Then Grandma squeezed Aurora's hand. Aurora squeezed Papa's hand. Papa squeezed Aunt Jo. The squeeze went all the way around, one hand at a time. Then the circle came back to Aurora. Everyone said the blessing together, loud and happy.

"The squeeze went all the way around," said Aurora. "It came back to me." Grandma smiled. "Yes. It goes around because we all hold hands." Aurora clapped. "We are lucky we have so many hands!"

After dinner, Grandma gave Aurora a pencil. Together they drew a big circle on paper. Grandma put a tiny hand in the circle for each person. Aurora counted them all. "One, two, three, four, five!" she said. Then she drew a line from hand to hand. "Look, Grandma. My squeeze will go here, and here, and here."

"Next Sunday, you can start the squeeze," said Grandma. Aurora jumped up and down. "I will squeeze your hand first!"

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Violet put on her red dress. Her family walked to the big temple house. Today was Diwali, the festival of lights.

Inside, small clay lamps glowed everywhere. Violet's grandma gave her a lamp. "Hold it flat," Grandma said. Violet held it very still. Then a man walked past. The air moved. The little flame went out. The lamp was dark now. Violet looked at her grandma's lamp. It was still lit. It sat by the wall, where the air was still.

"I know why," Violet said. "The wind blew it out. The wind did not blow yours."

"Try again," said Grandma. They found a quiet spot by the wall. Grandma lit the wick with a match. Violet set her lamp down next to Grandma's. The flame stood up small and bright. Nobody walked past. Nobody blew. The light stayed on.

"It is not scary now," Violet said. "It stays when the wind stays away."

Grandma smiled and held her hand. The two little lamps glowed side by side all evening.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Violet was late for school. She had missed her breakfast. Her tummy made a little rumble.

At circle time, Miss Kim sang the counting song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." All the children clapped. Violet clapped too. But her mouth would not say the words.

Miss Kim smiled. "Sing with us, Violet. Just say the words after me."

Violet tried. "One, two, three, four, six, eight, nine," she said. The boy next to her giggled softly.

Violet tried again. "One, two, three, four, six," she said. "It went wrong!"

Miss Kim clapped her hands. "Let's go slow. Say each word as I sing it."

"One," sang Miss Kim. "One," sang Violet. "Two." "Two." They went all the way to six. Then Miss Kim stopped.

"Now comes the next word," said Miss Kim. "Watch my mouth."

"Seven," said Miss Kim. "Seven!" said Violet. The word fit right after six, like a puzzle piece.

They sang the whole song. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Violet said every word. Every word fit in its place.

"I did it!" said Violet. "Seven comes after six. That is why it went wrong."

Miss Kim gave her a cracker, and Violet ate it all up. Then Miss Kim sang the song one more time, just for her.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Clara sat at the little table. It was lunch time at school. Her soup was big and hot. Her friend Ben had a small cup. His soup was cold already.

"Mine is too hot," said Clara. She wanted to eat it now.

She looked out the window. A wild bird sat on the sill. It flapped one wing, then the other. The wind blew. The wing went up and down, up and down. Fast air moved over it.

Clara had an idea. Air can cool things. She picked up her spoon. She blew on the soup. One big blow. Two big blows. Three big blows. She blew slow. The steam still rose. She blew fast, like the wild wind. The steam went away.

Ben watched her. He tried it too. He blew on his cold soup. "Mine stays cold," he said.

"Yes," said Clara. "Cold stays cold. Blowing is for hot."

The teacher came with bread. Clara took one bite. "Just right now," she said. She smiled and blew a little kiss to the wild bird. The bird flapped both wings and flew away.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
William was at summer camp. There was one big red truck. William wanted it first.

He grabbed the truck. His friend Max said, "No! My turn." Max started to cry. William felt sad too.

The teacher came over. She had two sand timers. One was big and one was small. She said, "When the sand runs down, it is a new turn."

William turned the big timer over. Sand fell down, bit by bit. He pushed the truck in the dirt. He made a long road for it. Max watched and waited.

Then the sand ran out. William gave Max the truck. Max turned the timer over. He pushed the truck now. William watched the sand fall.

At snack time, William sat with Max. They shared a bowl of crackers. William said, "The sand fell down, so it was your turn." Max smiled a friendly smile and said, "You waited for me."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Rehmat went to the bank with Mama. Rehmat wore her red coat. The coat was not zipped. Rehmat wanted to zip it all by herself.

She pulled the zipper. It did not move. She pulled it again. Still nothing! Rehmat looked down. The zipper slide was at the very bottom. It was not in the little slot yet. The zipper had to sit in the slot first.

Rehmat sat on the bank floor. She pushed the bottom of the coat into the slot. Click! It went in. Then she pulled the zipper up, up, up. Zip! The coat closed all the way to her chin.

"Cold air can not get in now," said Rehmat. Mama laughed. "Look at you! Zipped up like a big girl." Rehmat opened the coat. Then she zipped it again, just for fun. Zip, zip, zip.

A man at the bank gave Rehmat a shiny red apple. "For the girl with the good zipper," he said. Rehmat held it in her warm, zipped pocket.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
story:
Luka was at summer camp. He saw a paint table. Red, yellow, and blue pots sat there. He wanted to paint a green frog. But there was no green paint. He felt shy about asking. So he sat down and watched.

His teacher came. She poured a little yellow. Then she poured a little blue. Luka waited. He dipped his brush. He tried it himself. He mixed yellow and blue together. The paint turned green!

"Look!" said Luka. "Yellow and blue make green." The teacher smiled. Luka painted his frog. He added big eyes. He added little feet. Then he dipped red and yellow. He mixed them. Now he had orange too. He painted a small orange hat on his frog.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Joshua stood at the little table in the school cooking room. Today he would make pancakes for his family. He poured flour, one cup, two cups. He cracked an egg. He added milk. Then he stirred and stirred. The batter looked like thick mud.

"Careful," said Teacher May. "Don't stir too fast." But Joshua stirred fast, and the batter flew out. Splatter! A naughty drop landed on his nose. Joshua laughed and laughed.

He stirred slowly this time, round and round. The batter stayed in the bowl. Teacher May poured it into the hot pan. One pancake, two pancakes, three pancakes, four. They smelled sweet and buttery. Joshua packed them in a box. "Mama, Dada, and me!" he said. He carried the box all the way to the door, sniffing the warm smell.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Charlie was at Sam's birthday party. There was a big red bumpy ball. Charlie wanted to kick it first.

Ben grabbed the bumpy ball at the same time. Charlie grabbed it too. She pulled hard. The ball hit her leg. It left a little scratch on her knee.

Dad knelt down next to her. "That scratch looks small," he said. "Let's find a way to play." Dad held up one hand. "We can count to ten. Then it is a new turn."

Charlie wiped her eyes. She held the ball. "One, two, three," she counted. Ben kicked the ball at ten. Then Charlie kicked it. The ball bounced over the cake table. Everyone laughed. Even Grandma jumped up to catch it.

"My turn went fast because I counted," said Charlie. She held the ball out to Ben. "You can go. I will wait."

Ben smiled big. The bumpy ball rolled and rolled across the grass.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Miles sat in the family car. He held his blanket tight. Today he would get his first big boy haircut. His tummy felt funny, but he marched up to the salon door anyway.

The hairdresser, Miss Jo, picked up a spray bottle. "Want to push it?" she asked. Miles pushed the button. Spritz, spritz! Water came out. His hair got wet. Wet hair stuck together in little dark points. Then Miss Jo cut with her scissors. Snip, snip. The wet pieces fell down like tiny rain drops. "Wet hair is easy to cut," Miles said. "It sticks in a line!"

Soon his hair was short and neat. Miles looked in the mirror. He saw a big boy with a big smile. At home he put his wet hands in his hair. "Mommy, wet makes it stay!" he said. Mommy laughed and hugged him tight.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Parker made a painting at school today. It was a red heart for his mom. It was her birthday gift.

"I want to take it now," said Parker.

Ms. Kim shook her head. "It is still wet. Wet paint makes spots on your bag."

Parker touched the paper. His finger came back red. He looked for his friend Leo. Leo was missing. Leo was home sick today. Yesterday Leo was here. Tomorrow he would come back.

Parker asked, "When will my painting be ready?"

Ms. Kim said, "Later. It needs time to dry."

So Parker waited. He played with blocks. He ate his snack. He looked at the painting again and again.

At last the paint was dry. The paper felt smooth. Parker held it up.

"Now I can bring it home," he said. "The paint dried because I waited."

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
story:
Anna lost her soft bunny at school. She looked by the swings. She looked by the sand. No bunny. "Where are you, bunny?" she said.

Anna sat down on the little bench. She thought hard. "I had bunny when I sat here," she said. "Then I put my jacket down." She picked up her red jacket. She had to fold it to go down the short slide. Something soft was inside. It was bunny! Bunny was hiding in the jacket all along.

"Bunny was in my jacket," said Anna. "Bunny was in my jacket!" She hugged bunny tight. Her friend Tom ran over. "I looked by the park fence," he said. "No bunny there." Anna smiled. "Bunny was with me," she said. "Let's go on the slide together." Anna held bunny's paw and off they went.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Milo went to the park with his dad. He saw a hoop on the grass. He wanted to toss a beanbag into it.

Milo threw the beanbag hard. It went past the hoop. It landed far away in the sand.

He tried again. This time he tossed it up, high and soft. The beanbag dropped down. It fell right in. "It goes in when I toss it up," said Milo.

Then Dad rolled him a big ball. Milo used one hand. The ball bumped his fingers and fell. He got up fast and felt dizzy for a second. Dad waited, then rolled the ball again.

Milo held out both hands. He hugged the ball to his chest. He caught it!

"You did it," said Dad. He clapped and clapped.

The park felt like Milo's whole world that day. After, Dad filled Milo's water cup. Milo drank it all. "Again," said Milo, holding out both hands.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: people's jobs and how a community works
fact: At a library, you can borrow books and take them home, but you must bring them back by a certain day so other people can read them too.
story:
Eli sits on the small red rug at daycare. Miss Pam holds up a book. It has a picture of a red truck on the front. "This book is from the library," she says. "We can take it home, but not for always."

Eli wants the truck book for always. He holds it tight. "My truck book," he says.

Miss Pam sits down next to him. "The library lets us borrow it," she says. "Borrow means we take it home, then bring it back. Other kids want to read it too."

Eli opens the book. He turns the pages from the front. The truck goes up a hill. Then the truck goes fast down the hill. At the top of the last page, the truck sleeps. "It ends!" says Eli. "How does it start again?" He turns back to the first page. The words sit in little rows. Miss Pam reads them out loud. The words tell the truck what to do.

Eli looks at the words. "The marks talk," he says. "They say truck!"

Eli takes the book home. His mom reads it three times. On the last page, Eli pats the truck. "Good night, truck."

The next day, Eli brings the book back to daycare. He gives it to Miss Pam. "The book is for the other kids now," he says. "They read it too." Then he picks a new one, a book about a big yellow duck. He sits on the rug and turns to page one. "Read the marks, please," he says.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Lena put on her fox apron. It had a big orange fox on the front. Today she would make pancakes for the whole family.

She mixed flour, milk and one egg. Mom reminded her, "Do not forget the little spoon of baking powder." But Lena forgot it.

She poured the mix into the warm pan. The pancake stayed flat. It looked like a sad little plate.

"Why is it flat?" Lena asked.

Mom held up the small tin. "Because we left this out. It makes pancakes puff up."

Lena stirred the baking powder in. She poured a new pancake. It puffed up big and fat. "It got fluffy because of the powder!" Lena said.

The stack grew tall. Lena set the table fast. Then she took a big breath and did her loudest yell. "Pancakes are ready!"

Dad came running. Lena pointed at the tall warm stack and grinned.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
story:
Lillian went to the cultural center with Mama and Papa. It was Diwali, the festival of lights. There were little clay lamps called diyas everywhere. Lillian wanted to light one all by herself.

Papa gave her a small diya. Lillian held the flame to the wick. It lit up. Then it went out. Lillian looked sad. She tried again. The wick lit up. Then it went out again.

The room was noisy with music and singing. Lillian looked at the big diyas on the table. Their flames stayed on and on. She looked at her diya. The oil was all gone. The big ones had lots of oil.

"The oil makes it stay on," Lillian said. Papa smiled. He poured more oil into her diya. Lillian lit the wick one more time. The little flame stood up tall. It stayed on. Lillian sat back and watched her light shine with all the others.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Henry jumped into the family car. "Are we at Grandma's yet?" he asked. "Not yet," said Dad. "Grandma lives far, far away. First we need gas." Henry buckled his shoe taps together and waited.

Dad drove and drove. The car made a funny cough. Then it slowed down. Dad pulled over at a gas station. "Why did the car stop?" Henry asked. "Because the tank is empty," said Dad. "Cars need gas to go."

Henry watched Dad put the nozzle in the tank. It made a glug, glug sound. Then Dad closed the little door on the car. "Full tank!" said Dad. "Now we can go again."

The car zoomed back onto the road. Henry saw a stormy sky with big gray clouds. Rain tapped on the window. Soon the rain stopped, and a rainbow came out. "We did it!" said Henry. Then he yawned and fell asleep. When he woke up, Grandma was waving at her door.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
story:
Ibrahim wants to play outside. He looks out the big window. "Oh no," he says. "Rainy today." Little drops tap the glass. Tap, tap, tap.

Mama comes to the window too. "Rainy days need boots," she says. Ibrahim runs to the shoe rack. He puts on his red boots. He remembers his hat with ears. He gets that too. But wait. His robot toy is on the porch! It is sitting in the rain.

Ibrahim opens the door. He walks out in his boots. Puddle, splash, puddle, splash. He picks up the robot. It is wet, but it still beeps. "Good robot!" says Ibrahim. He hugs it dry with his towel.

Then the wind blows. Whoosh! His hat almost flies away. "Windy too!" says Ibrahim. He holds his hat with one hand. He holds the robot with the other hand. Mama lifts him up. "All safe and dry," she says. The robot beeps a happy little beep.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
story:
Evelyn lived in a little house with a red door. She wanted to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" all by herself. Mama sang it, and Evelyn tried. The words fell out in a jumble.

Then Mama clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Slow and steady, like a clock. Evelyn clapped too. Her claps went fast, fast, fast. "Too fast," said Mama with a smile. "The song walks, it does not run."

Evelyn looked at her red block on the floor. She put it down. She listened first. Clap, clap, clap. Then she copied Mama. Clap, clap, clap. Now her hands went the same speed! The claps fit the song.

Evelyn clapped and sang at the very same time. "Twin-kle, twin-kle, lit-tle star." Each word sat on a clap. The whole rhyme came out, from start to end, with no jumble at all. Mama picked up the teddy bear and bounced him to the beat.

Evelyn gasped. "Mama! The claps are walking. The song walks too. That is why it works!" She hugged the teddy tight. "Teddy, now you sing." She tapped his soft paw, clap, clap, clap.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
story:
Kinsley ran to the slide at the park. Mom sat on a bench close by. The slide was long and slippery. Kinsley wanted to go down it, but the ladder looked high.

"Help, please," Kinsley said. Mom came right over and held her hand. Kinsley climbed up, one square step at a time. At the top, she sat down. Whoosh! She slid all the way to the bottom.

Then a boy bumped into her. "Sorry," he said. "It is okay," said Kinsley. She stood up and brushed off her knees. Mom clapped. "Thank you, Mom," Kinsley said.

"I slid fast because the slide is slippery," said Kinsley. Mom smiled. Then they walked home to cook lunch together. "Pasta, please!" said Kinsley.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
story:
Paisley came home with a goldfish. His name was Dot. He swam in his little bowl.

Paisley was worried. "Is Dot hungry?" she asked. Dad was there to help.

Paisley poured in lots of food. "This is yummy food," she said. But Dot did not eat it all. The food sank down. The water got cloudy and yucky. Dot hid behind his little castle.

Dad said, "Let's fix it." They scooped out the extra food. They put in fresh, clean water. Soon the water was clear again.

Paisley saw Dot come out of his castle. He wiggled his tail. He blew a tiny bubble.

"Now I know," said Paisley. "Too much food makes the water dirty." Dad smiled. "Just a little pinch each day."

That night the moon shone in the window. Paisley gave Dot one small pinch. Dot gobbled it all up.

"Good night, Dot," said Paisley. Dot blew one more bubble.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Georgia stood by the red barn. She wore her loose sun hat. The hat was too big for her head.

"I want to know my five senses," Georgia said to Grandma.

Grandma smiled. "Let's find them together."

Georgia sniffed the air. "I smell hay with my nose," she said.

Then the hen went cluck, cluck. Georgia covered her ears. "I hear the hen with my ears."

Grandma picked a ripe strawberry. Georgia put it in her mouth. "I taste sweet with my tongue."

A soft lamb walked near. Georgia touched its wool. "I feel soft with my hands."

"Now one more," said Grandma.

Georgia looked around. She saw a yellow duck. "I see the duck with my eyes!"

Grandma clapped. "Five senses. You found them all."

Georgia's loose hat slipped down over her eyes. "Now I see nothing!" she said.

Grandma lifted the hat up. The sun came back. Georgia saw the yellow duck again, splashing in the little pond.

"Hello, duck," said Georgia. "I see you."

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
story:
Olivia stood by the coat hooks at school. It was cold outside. Her teacher said, "Coats on, everyone."

Olivia pushed her arms into her sleeves. The coat was on. Now came the zipper. She pulled the pull tab up. Nothing happened. The zipper did not move. She looked down. The two sides of her coat were apart.

She tried again, slowly. First she pushed the little metal tab into the slot at the bottom. Click. The two sides were stuck together now. Then she pulled the pull tab up. The zipper went up, up, up. "I did it!" said Olivia.

Her friend Sam was still pulling at his zipper. His coat was different. It had buttons. Olivia waited by the door. The clock on the wall ticked while Sam pushed each button through its hole. One, two, three.

At last Sam was done. "Ready," he said. They held hands and walked out into the cold.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Axel sat at the dinner table. He had ten green peas on his plate. Big news! He wanted to count them all by himself.

"One, two, three, four," he said. Then he stopped. What came after four? He could not remember. His tooth felt funny when he smiled, so he covered his mouth with his hand.

Dad held up his fingers. He tapped them one by one. "One, two, three, four," said Dad. He held up the next finger. He waited.

"Five!" shouted Axel. "Then six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" He pointed at each pea as he said each word. Every pea got one word. No pea was missing.

Then Axel counted his spoonfuls of rice. One, two, three, all the way to the last bite. He did not forget a single word now.

"Can I count your peas too, Dad?" he asked.

"Ten carrots coming up," said Dad.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Luka sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. He wanted the gold sticker on the desk. But first, the doctor said, he had to try five things. Luka looked at the fish tank. Two small fish swim round and round. He saw them with his eyes. One.

Next came his ears. The doctor rang a little bell. Ding, ding. Then she said, "Close your eyes. Can you still hear it?" Luka shut his eyes tight. Ding. "Yes!" he said. "My ears work without my eyes!" Two.

He sniffed a sweet orange. His nose knew it. Three. He stuck out his tongue. The doctor put a tiny drop on it. Sour! He made a funny face. Four.

Then Luka touched the sticker. It felt smooth and shiny. Five. The doctor gave it to him. On the wall was a poster of a tree. Luka pointed at it. "What is the bottom part called?" he asked. The doctor smiled. "That is the root," she said. Luka stuck the gold star right on his shirt.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Jordan sat at the big table. The game was on the huge screen. Everyone wore blue hats. Dad's boot tapped the floor fast. Jordan colored his menu with a red crayon. He colored a big blue ball, just like on the screen.

But Jordan could not hear the game. He looked at the TV. The players ran. Their mouths moved. No sound came out at all. Jordan wanted to hear the roars. He wanted to hear the whistle. He put down his crayon. Then he saw small words at the bottom of the screen. The words told who scored! The score numbers changed too. Now Jordan knew what happened. The TV was quiet because the restaurant had it on mute. The words helped him watch.

"Look, the score says two to two!" Jordan shouted. Everyone cheered. Mom ordered frozen yogurt for the win. Jordan held up his menu. "I colored the ball for luck," he said. Dad gave him a high five. The whistle blew. Blue team scored! The score changed to three to two. "See, the numbers know!" said Jordan.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Iris wanted to wash her hands all by herself. Dad was folding towels in the hall. She pulled a stool to the sink. The tap was shiny and silver. She turned it with both hands.

The water came out fast. It was cold at first. Then it got hot. Very hot. Iris pulled her hands back quick. "Ow," she said. She turned the blue tap instead. The water turned cool again. "Hot water can hurt," she whispered. "I will use the cool side."

Dad heard her small voice. He came in fast. "Are you okay, Iris?" he asked. "The water got hot," said Iris. "So I moved my hands. Then I made it cool." Dad smiled a big smile. "You learn fast," he said.

He stayed close while she washed. She rubbed the soap on her hands. Bubbles went pop, pop, pop. The water stayed cool and nice. Dad gave her a small towel. Iris dried her hands all by herself. "I did it," she said. Dad clapped his hands. Iris hung the towel on the shiny hook.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Liam sat in the school computer lab. A big tablet lay on the table. He wanted to draw a red truck on it.

Liam pushed the screen with his finger. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark and cool. He waited. Then he saw the round button on the bottom edge. He pressed it and counted slowly, one, two, three. The screen lit up bright. "I did it," Liam said.

He looked for the drawing app. It was a little square with a crayon on it. He tapped it with one finger. The app opened. Liam picked the red color and drew a big truck. He drew two round wheels. He made the line tight and small for the window. His teacher smiled.

Now it was time for snack. Liam had to put the tablet away. He pressed the round button on the bottom again. The screen went dark. He slid the tablet back onto the shelf, next to the other tablets.

Liam looked at his teacher. "When I press the bottom, the light goes out," he said. She nodded. Liam patted the tablet gently, like a sleepy cat, and ran off to find his crackers.

activity: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
knowledge_domain: to throw a beanbag into a hoop and catch a large ball with both hands
story:
Madison stood at the big running track. Her beanbag was shaped like a pink pig. She wanted to toss it into a hoop on the ground.

Madison threw the pig. It fell short. She tried again. Still short. Then she held her arm straight and long, like a stick. She let go at the end. The pig flew far and landed in the hoop. "My arm was straight, so it went far!" she said.

Next, Dad rolled a big ball to her. Madison tried to catch it with one hand. The ball bumped her fingers and fell. "Why did it fall?" she asked. "I only used one hand." So she held out both hands. Dad rolled the ball again. It went right into them. Madison hugged the big ball and laughed. The pig beanbag sat in the hoop, and Madison jumped up and down.
